title: Judges 15:9–20
context: The Philistines invade Judah to capture Samson, and the men of Judah, accepting Philistine rule, hand their own judge over bound. At Lehi the LORD's Spirit comes on Samson, the ropes fall away, and he strikes a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone. Exhausted and thirsty, he calls on the LORD for the first time in the narrative, and God answers by opening a spring. The chapter closes by noting that Samson judged Israel twenty years.

verses.text: Then the Philistines went up, encamped in Judah, and spread themselves in Lehi.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines camp in Judah and spread out in Lehi. Arminian readers note that Samson's private feud now brings an invading force against his own people, showing how one person's choices affect a whole community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conflict widening as God sets the stage for a public deliverance. The Philistine advance, intended to crush Samson, becomes the occasion of their own defeat under God's providence.

verses.text: The men of Judah said, “Why have you come up against us?” They said, “We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he has done to us.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines want to "do to him as he has done to us." Arminian readers note that both sides speak the language of tit-for-tat retaliation, the same logic Samson used, and neither seeks justice from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Philistines' words mirror Samson's own (verse 11). Scripture shows the self-perpetuating nature of human vengeance, which only God's intervention can interrupt and overrule.

verses.text: Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave in Etam’s rock, and said to Samson, “Don’t you know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?” He said to them, “As they did to me, so I have done to them.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Don't you know that the Philistines are rulers over us?" Three thousand men of Judah come to bind their own deliverer. Arminian readers see a people resigned to oppression, unwilling to trust God and resist.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the sad contrast with Judah's bold leadership in Judges 1. The tribe of promise has grown content under foreign rule, and God's rescue will come despite his people's lack of faith, not because of it.

verses.text: They said to him, “We have come down to bind you, that we may deliver you into the hand of the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson asks Judah to swear they will not attack him themselves. Arminian readers note that he submits to his own people rather than fight them, a rare moment of restraint that shows his choices were genuinely his.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson allows himself to be handed over. Some see a faint pattern of the deliverer rejected and bound by his own people, though the text does not draw that connection explicitly.

verses.text: They spoke to him, saying, “No, but we will bind you securely and deliver you into their hands; but surely we will not kill you.” They bound him with two new ropes, and brought him up from the rock.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah binds Samson "with two new ropes" and promises not to kill him. Arminian readers see the tragedy of a people more willing to bind their deliverer than their oppressors, a pattern of misplaced loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the strongest ropes Judah can supply mean nothing before God's purpose. The binding sets up a display of divine power that leaves no doubt about who gives the victory.

verses.text: When he came to Lehi, the Philistines shouted as they met him. Then the LORD’s Spirit came mightily on him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that was burned with fire; and his bands dropped from off his hands.
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD's Spirit came mightily on him," and the ropes become like burned flax. Arminian readers note that Samson's strength is explicitly God's gift, not his own, even though he often uses it in self-directed ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the decisive moment is the Spirit's action. The same phrase marks Samson's earlier feats (14:6, 19). God's sovereign empowering, not Samson's character, is the source of deliverance.

verses.text: He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, put out his hand, took it, and struck a thousand men with it.
verses.arminianNotes: A fresh donkey jawbone becomes a weapon against a thousand men. Some Arminian interpreters, recalling the honey from the lion's carcass (14:8–9), ask how carefully Samson kept his consecration, though Numbers 6:6 speaks only of "a dead body."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a crude, unclean instrument becomes the means of a great victory. God often works through weak or unlikely means so that the glory belongs to him, though Samson's own carelessness remains real.

verses.text: Samson said, “With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps on heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck a thousand men.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson's victory song is a wordplay in Hebrew, since the words for donkey and heap sound alike. Arminian readers note that the song celebrates his own strength and mentions God not at all, a revealing silence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note that the song is self-focused. They see this as the setup for verse 18, where Samson's thirst humbles him and moves him to acknowledge that the deliverance came from the LORD.

verses.text: When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone out of his hand; and that place was called Ramath Lehi.
verses.arminianNotes: Samson throws the jawbone away and the place is named Ramath Lehi, usually understood as "hill of the jawbone." Arminian readers see a memorial of what God did, even if Samson's own song credited himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see place names in Judges as lasting witnesses. The site preserves the memory of the victory, and later readers would know whose Spirit really won it, as verse 14 makes plain.

verses.text: He was very thirsty, and called on the LORD and said, “You have given this great deliverance by the hand of your servant; and now shall I die of thirst, and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
verses.arminianNotes: "You have given this great deliverance by the hand of your servant." Here Samson calls on the LORD for the first time in the account. Arminian readers see real humility emerge through need, a turning toward God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson now credits God with the victory and calls himself God's servant. They see grace at work, as God uses physical weakness to bring his servant to acknowledge dependence on him.

verses.text: But God split the hollow place that is in Lehi, and water came out of it. When he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived. Therefore its name was called En Hakkore, which is in Lehi, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: God splits the hollow at Lehi and water flows; the spring is named En Hakkore, usually understood as "spring of the one who called." Arminian readers see prayer answered, a real exchange between God and his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's faithful provision for his chosen judge. The spring's name makes prayer and answer a lasting memorial, showing that the one who calls on the LORD is sustained by God's free kindness.

verses.text: He judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes: "He judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines." Arminian readers note that the Philistines still rule; Samson's career offers relief but not full liberation, reflecting a people not yet turned fully to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same summary returns in 16:31. Samson's judgeship is real yet limited, fitting 13:5, "He shall begin to save Israel." God's deliverance unfolds in stages toward a greater fulfillment.
